title: Molten Salt Treated Cu Foam Catalyst for Selective Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction
abstract: The electrochemical reduction of CO2 is a promising route to convert waste products to valuable chemicals. Search for suitable and efficient CO2 reduction electrocatalysts with high C2:C1 selectivity holds great promise. Herein, for the first time we have developed a molten salt oxidized method to modify the morphology and oxidation state of a Cu-foam catalyst. The catalyst displayed a current density of 30 mAcm 2 ( 1.4 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode) and an ethylene/ methane ratio of 870. We provide insight into the improved performance of the catalysts by cross section scanning transmission electron microscopy and quasi in situ soft X-ray spectroscope, which show that copper oxides are surprisingly reconstructed with Cu (I) and Cu (0) on the surface during the reaction. First principle calculations also demonstrate that the partly reduced Cu2O (111) surface has a high reactivity and selectivity for C2+ products. Furthermore, the molten salt treated catalysts could be applied to the direct synthesis of multi-carbon fuels, including C3-C4 compounds in high CO2 pressure electrocatalytic reduction. Our results demonstrate that molten salt are both the oxidizing agent and reaction medium, which is a promising approach for synthesis of highly active CO2 electrocatalysts, which may open a new way for industrial application.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
With a growing population and increasing consumption of fossil fuels, the concentration of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere has risen rapidly in the past decades. Thus, techniques for the efficient fixation and utilization of CO2 are highly desirable. Recently, electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) has received a great deal of attention because of its potential to produce value added chemicals.[1] In addition, the electrochemical conversion pathway is applicable as a future energy storage system, which is increasingly in demand
due to the imbalanced supply of renewable energy sources.[2]
To achieve economic feasibility of the electrochemical CO2 conversion technique, it is required to produce market valuable chemicals, such as ethylene (C2H4), ethane (C2H6) and alcohols. Among the possible products, C2+ hydrocarbons have received much attention in view of their commercial value.[3]
Copper-based catalysts are the most promising materials for selective reduction of CO2 to multi-carbon hydrocarbons since they had a moderate binding energy with carbon monoxide.[4] High selectivity toward C2+ products, including C2H4, C2H5OH, and C3H7OH has been demonstrated using Cubased catalysts.[5] Researchers have tried to regulate the number of active sites on oxide-derived Cu catalysts, which have been created by a number of different processes including O2 plasma treatment,
[5b] electrodeposition of cuprous oxide (Cu2O), [6] reduction of copper salts,[3b] metal-ion cycling,[5c] and thermal treatment of metallic Cu in air.[7] The previous experimental and modeling efforts have also highlighted the importance of catalyst surface morphology on C2+ selectivity in CO2RR.
[8] These materials were synthesized from the reduction of thermally oxidized Cu or electrodeposited Cu2O on the surface of the catalysts. Mechanisms underlying the improved selectivity often involve the initial material oxidation state.[4e,9] For example, residual subsurface oxygen,[10] grain boundaries,[11] and unconverted Cu (I) states[3b,5b] were reported to enhance CO adsorption and reduce the energy barrier for CO CO coupling. All the above studies indicate that a nanostructured morphology, roughness and copper oxidation state have a significant effect on the catalytic activity and selectivity for the CO2RR.

Here, we report a surface engineering approach for preparation of Cu-foam derived catalyst that enables us to tune the hydrocarbon selectivity during CO2RR using a molten salt process. The key development is the use of a molten nitrate as both the oxidizing agent and reaction medium. We are able to control the oxidation state and morphology of a Cu-form surface to provide a Cu (I) oxide surface using facile chemical oxidation processes.[12] High C2+ selectivity for carbon products was observed, with a faradaic efficiencies (FE) of 22.3% for ethylene and a ratio of C2H4 to CH4 up to 870. Furthermore, the high CO2 pressure electrocatalytic reduction experiment showed it could produce C3 and C4 compounds. Quasi in situ soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) found that the surface of the used catalyst was reconstructed with existence of Cu (I) and Cu (0). It is synergy effects between the surface Cu (I) and surface Cu (0) to improve significantly the kinetics and thermodynamics of both CO2 activation and CO dimerization, while making C1 unfavorable, thereby boosting the efficiency and selectivity of

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Our strategy is to control a formation of Cu2O surface structure on the Cu-foam from a molten salt oxide method developed here. In Figure 1a, Cu-foams and potassium nitrate were considered as reactant, by regulating the time of the oxidation to obtain desired oxidation states of copper. The polished Cufoam and the Cu-foam after molten salt treatment were examined by XRD. It can be seen that the Cu-foam match well with metallic Cu (JCPDS 65-9743), the three main peaks are corresponded with (111), (200), (220), as shown in Figure 1b.[14]
When the Cu-foam treated in the molten salt for 1 h, the new phase was present, it can be indexed with Cu2O with (110), (111), (200).[7] However, after 2 h reaction time, CuO was appeared as indicated in supporting information Figure S1.[15]
To further study the electronic and geometric structure of the catalysts, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was employed. It is well known that X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES) spectrum is sensitive to the chemical state of the investigated elements.[16] The Cu K XANES is very similar to that of Cu metal, but the weak spectral from Cu (I) can be still detected especially in the derivative curves of the XANES spectrum, as show in Figure S2.[17] However, the XANES at the transition metal K-edge has a typical probing depth of micrometres. In order to obtain the status of Cu ions at the surface, we performed soft XAS measurements at the transition metal L2,3-edge using a total electron yield (TEY) mode, which has a typical exploring depth of 2–5 nm and is very sensitive to the Cu valence state and the Cu O Cu networks.[18] The
11928ChemistrySelect 2020, 5, 11927–11933 © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH
Wiley VCH Dienstag, 13.10.2020 2038 / 181519 [S. 11928/11933] 1
catalyst samples were stored and transferred under the vacuum package prior to the spectroscopy measurements to minimize the changes of the surface.[19] Figure 1c shows the Cu L3-edge XAS spectra of the molten salt treated sample and CuO, Cu2O, Cu-foil references for comparison. The spectral profile and the energy position of the molten salt treated Cu-foam sample are very similar to those of Cu2O demonstrating Cu (I) state. The formation of Cu (I) is further confirmed by the Cu LMM Auger spectra in Figure 1d.
In order to depict the effect of molten salt treatment on the morphology, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) measurement was carried out. It showed that the Cu-foam had porous structure under the condition of low magnification (Figure S3a). However, it had a smooth surface under higher magnification conditions (Figure S3b), and there is no layered structure. It was also found that the morphology of the Cu-foam-ms-1 h was nearly the same as to that of pristine Cu-foam, exhibiting a porous structure, as shown in Figure 2a and Figure S4a. Interestingly, the surface of Cu-foam-ms-1 h shows a clear change of roughness, in Figure 2b and Figure S4b. To gain further information on the structure and chemical state of the molten salt-treated Cu-foam, we used a focused ion beam (FIB) to cut ultra-thin specimens for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterizations of cross-sections (Methods), the results were presented in Figure 2c. In Figure 2c, the Cu-foamms-1 h was divided into two layers. Combining with EDS, one
11929ChemistrySelect 2020, 5, 11927–11933 © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH
Wiley VCH Dienstag, 13.10.2020 2038 / 181519 [S. 11929/11933] 1
can clearly observe that the oxygen is on the top layer, therefore it was copper oxide; while the bottom is only metallic copper. Also, SAED pattern and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) on the top layer in Figure 2d show the d=2.43 Å, which corresponds to the (111) of Cu2O, and the bottom layer has d=2.09 Å in Figure 2e, which well stands for the Cu (111). We can conclude that the molten salt treated Cu-foams form a layer of cuprous oxide on the surface.
To understand the performance of Cu foam and Cu foamms-1 h on CO2 reduction, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed (Figure S5). It was observed that the H2 evolution and probably CO2 reduction initiated at approximately - 0.8 V (vs. RHE). The geometrical current density under various potential is presented in Figure 3a and Figure S6, it can be seen that the current densities of Cu-foam-ms-1 h ranged from 10 to 40 mAcm 2 depending on applied potential, and is higher than that of Cu-foam at the same applied potential (Figure S7). This result indicated that the molten salt treated Cu-foam had a positive effect on the CO2RR.
To get the product distribution of CO2 reduction of both Cu foam and Cu foam-ms-1 h, the electrolysis was conducted at a variety of constant potentials from 0.8 to 1.7 V (versus RHE) for 40 min. The electrolytic cell is purged with CO2 constantly and vented directly into the gas sampling loop of a gas chromatograph to examine the composition of gaseous products. Liquid products were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography analysis after the electrolysis was finished. All the data were repeated three times and averaged.
It is well-established that H2 evolution is a competing reaction with CO2 reduction in CO2-saturated electrolytes, therefore the production of H2 was also measured during electrolysis. Figure 3b and Figure S8 show the overall product selectivity of the Cu foam. The FE for H2 of Cu-foam was found to range from 30 to 60% at different applied potential between 0.8 V and 1.2 V (versus RHE), and achieved a relatively stable value of about 40% with increasing the potential. The major CO2RR products of Cu foam are C1 products including CO (8%) and formate (60%) at –0.8 V versus RHE, and CH4, which gradually increased at higher negative potentials (10% FE at –1.3 V versus RHE). But C2+ products, including C2H4, C2H6, and C3H6, were few, and their FEs were no more than 10%. It means that the Cu-foam had low FE of C2+, which is consistent with other reports for copper-based catalyst.[20]
However, the distribution of products has changed significantly when Cu-foam-ms-1 h was used during CO2RR. For example, the FE of H2 was found to range from 35% to 42% depending on applied potential (Figure S9) and the FE of hydrocarbon was improved greatly. The FE of C2H4 reach a maximum at 22.3% at 1.4 V (versus RHE) and it also had nonnegligible C3 and C4 compounds. The FEs of CO and formate decreased when the applied potential increased at higher negative potentials, and there was nearly no CH4 formed as shown in Figure 3c. It can be concluded that the Cu-foam-ms1 h had an obvious advantage for producing olefin. Interestingly, the molten salt treated Cu-foam also had C3+ product as shown in Figure S10 and Figure S11 with about 0.22% of the
11930ChemistrySelect 2020, 5, 11927–11933 © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH
Wiley VCH Dienstag, 13.10.2020 2038 / 181519 [S. 11930/11933] 1
C3H6 at 1.2 V (versus RHE), while at 0.9 V (versus RHE) the C4H8 appeared. More interestingly, the ratio of C2H4 to CH4 was as high as 871 using Cu-foam-ms-1 h as show in Figure 3(d), and this is higher than that reported for the CO2RR in 0.1 M KHCO3. [3b,21]
As the Cu-foam-ms-1 h had more C2+ products, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the structure of Cu-foam-ms1 h is altered under CO2RR operation. In order to investigate this hypothesis, firstly we studied the change of the Cu foam after CO2RR treatment. The XRD in Figure S12 shows the intensity of Cu-foam after 40 min CO2RR treatment decreased comparing with before treated. According to Scheler’s equation, we calculate the crystallite size of Cu-foam and Cu-foamafter at (111) is 22.52 nm, 9.17 nm, respectively. The SEM in Figure S13 showed the particle morphology of the catalyst remained after CO2RR, while the surface became wrinkles. However, the Cu-foam-ms-1 h after CO2RR had different feature, the XRD in Figure S14 indicated that the Cu-foam-ms1 h was almost reduced to Cu metal, and small content of Cu2O remained at 2θ of 37° corresponding with (111), which could be further confirmed in Figure S15.
In order to provide insight into the valence change at surface of Cu-foam-ms-1 h during CO2RR, we performed quasi in situ soft XAS measurements of Cu-foam-ms-1 h catalyst at 1.4 V (versus RHE) as a function of the time during CO2 reduction. As depicted in Figure 4a, all spectra were normalized at energy position just below the Cu–L2 edge. We found that
the spectral weight of the Cu (I) related peak at 934 eV reduced with increasing the reaction time. During the first 2 min of reaction, the majority of the sample was in the Cu+ oxidation state. After a further reaction for 20 min, the amount of the Cu+ decreased. But, the spectral of the Cu (I) still exists in the sample after 40 minutes and is between Cu2O and Cu metal references as shown in Figure 4a. We can conclude that the Cu (I) content exist in material under CO2RR reaction in agreement with previous results.[3b,5a, d] Then we performed a long-term stability of the Cu-foam-ms-1 h for CO2RR in 24 h, as shown in Figure S16. We can confirm that the catalyst still had a good stability after 24 h. The morphology of Cu-foam-ms-1 h after CO2RR was the similar to that of Cu-foam as shown in Figure S17. The surface exhibits the coarse porous with many cracks. This means that after CO2RR the surface becomes very rough. From TEM of the FIB sample in Figure 4b, one can find that the catalyst can be divided into two layers. The SAED of the surface is a ring, which indicate the polycrystalline nanoparticles were generated. The inner ring is the (111) of Cu2O, and the brightest ring is the (111) of the Cu, which showed the surface had been reconstructed. In conclusion, the surface structure of Cu-foam-ms-1 h after reaction was reconstructed with Cu (0) and Cu (I), and that may be the activity site of the C2+ compounds.
We have performed the first principle calculations to figure out the activity of different surface state of Cu (111), Cu2O (111), and partly reduced Cu2O (111). Cu2O (111) surface with
11931ChemistrySelect 2020, 5, 11927–11933 © 2020 Wiley-VCH GmbH
Wiley VCH Dienstag, 13.10.2020 2038 / 181519 [S. 11931/11933] 1
oxygen vacancies (VO) is modelled to simulate the partly reduced Cu2O (111) surface. Pure Cu (111) has a clear metallic property without band gap as shown in Figure 4c. The electron can transfer to adsorbates easily.[13a,22] Pure Cu2O (111) in Figure 4e has a small band gap and high density of state near the Fermi level. The partly reduced Cu2O (111) surface in Figure 4d has a relative weak density state at Ef as compared with Cu (111), but much higher density state just below Ef than both pure Cu (111) and Cu2O (111), indicating a higher activity to transfer electrons to CO2. This is in agreement with the experimental results that partly reduced Cu2O (111) has a high reactivity and selectivity for C2+ products. Surface structure and detailed calculation are presented in the supporting information in Figure S18.
Having established that Cu-foam-ms-1 h is able to catalyse the CO2 reduction to C2+, we then explore the catalytic activity in high CO2 pressure electrocatalytic reduction. As the solubility of CO2 in water at standard conditions is low leading to a significant mass transfer limitation, which is one of character to limit the selectivity of the different product.[23] We explored the origin of the pressure on the Cu-foam and Cu-foam-ms-1 h, the electrochemical experiment was described in the experimental section and the results were shown in Figure 5. Apart from hydrogen, the major CO2RR products of Cu-foam sample are C1 compound, including formate (42.5%), CO (37.5%), and CH4 (7.5%), and the C2 is mainly C2H6 (at most 2.5%) and C2H4 (reach about 12.5%), while the C3+ is little. On the contrary, the major CO2RR products of Cu-foam-ms-1 h is obvious different. Its main products are mainly gas phase compounds, for example the FE of CO was 41% and that of CH4 is 2.5%. Furthermore, it has more C2+ compounds; the FE of C2H6 at Cufoam-ms-1 h is 5 times higher than that of Cu-foam, the FE of C2H4 reach about 30%, which is 2.5 times than the pristine Cufoam. More important the Cu-foam-ms-1 h can generate C3 and C4 compounds, while other high CO2 pressure experiment in the references C1 was dominating. [24,25]

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we used a molten salt method to control the oxidation of Cu-foam and obtain the catalyst with a skeleton structure of Cu2O. The catalyst exhibits a current density of 30 mAcm 2 ( 1.4 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode) and reaches the ratio of C2H4 to CH4 as high as 871 in 0.1 M KHCO3. In high CO2 presses reaction, it found that the molten salt treated catalysts could be applied to the direct synthesis of multi-carbon fuels, including C3-C4 compounds. After reaction the surface of catalyst had reconstruction include Cu2O and Cu might as an activity site for CO2RR. First principle calculations also demonstrate that part reduced Cu2O had a positive effect on the selection of C2+ products. We propose that the surface reconstruction with Cu (0) and Cu (I) can be further enhance both selectivity and current density for electrochemical CO2 conversion to value-added chemicals.
Supporting Information Summary
The supporting information includes the detailed procedure to obtain the electrodes, the characterization parameters of the electrodes, and the evaluation of Cu-based electrodes performance on CO2RR. XRD, SEM image, FIB images, XAS, cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometric measurements, product analysis, theoretical calculation details are also provided.
